subject: Business Models
title: Price Creep
description: A quick win: understand Price Creep.

hook.text: Netflix launched at $7.99/month in 2010. By 2024, its standard plan costs $15.49. Nearly doubled.

buildup.text: Subscription companies raise prices 5-10% annually. Each increase is small enough to avoid mass cancellations.

discovery.text: The 'boiling frog' effect: gradual increases go unnoticed until the total price shocks you.

twist.text: Spotify hasn't raised US prices for most of its life—and it's still unprofitable. Price creep is necessary.

climax.text: The tension is real: raise too slowly and die; raise too fast and subscribers flee.

punchline.text: $7.99 became $15.49. Small annual hikes add up over a decade.

quiz.question: Why is gradual price creep effective for subscription companies?

details.summary: Price creep describes the gradual increase of subscription prices over time, often in small increments designed to minimize cancellations. Netflix has raised prices from $8 to $23 over a decade..
details.whyItMatters: Price creep is a primary driver of subscription fatigue and churn. While each individual increase seems small, compounded over years they significantly change the value proposition..
takeaways: Small annual price increases compound significantly over subscriber lifetimes
Each increase raises churn risk as the value-to-price ratio shifts
Successful price increases are paired with visible feature additions

faq.question: Why do subscription companies continuously raise prices?
faq.answer: Content and infrastructure costs increase over time. Investors expect revenue growth, and price increases are easier than subscriber growth. Inflation erodes real revenue. Companies test price sensitivity and find that most subscribers tolerate small increases without canceling.

faq.question: How much price increase can subscription businesses implement before churn spikes?
faq.answer: Research shows 5-10% annual increases are generally tolerable. Increases above 15% trigger significant churn spikes. Consumers accept increases better when paired with new features or content. Grandfathering existing subscribers temporarily can smooth the transition.
